The Willow warbler (Phylloscopus trochilus) is a small migratory passerine that exhibits a life history closely tied to the temperate breeding seasons of its Palaearctic range. Females typically produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], laying between six and seven eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = between six and seven eggs per nesting attempt]. The eggs are incubated by the female alone, and under the stable thermal conditions of the nest, which are maintained at approximately 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the embryos develop over a period of 13 days [ab = 13 days] before hatching. This incubation duration is consistent with values reported for other small Phylloscopus warblers. The newly hatched nestlings are altricial, with a wet weight at birth recorded at only 1.05 grams [Wwb = 1.05 grams], a modest mass that reflects the relatively small energy reserve available in the egg. This initial mass places the young among the lighter hatchlings for a passerine of its eventual adult size, necessitating intense parental provisioning from the moment of hatching.

Following the hatching event, the nestling phase in the Willow warbler is a period of rapid somatic development and mass gain. When the ambient conditions are within the typical active metabolic temperature range of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the young achieve fledging status at 13 days after hatching [tx = 13 days after hatching], a point at which the developing chick has attained sufficient flight feather maturation to depart the nest. This rapid progression from an altricial hatchling to a fledgling is characteristic of many northern-latitude passerines facing a compressed breeding window. During this nestling period, the parents make constant foraging trips to meet the energetic demands of the brood. The ultimate wet weight of a fully developed adult Willow warbler is approximately 10 grams [Wwi = approximately 10 grams], a value that falls within the broader published range of 7 to 15 grams for the species. This relatively low adult mass imposes significant constraints on the birds' thermoregulatory capacity and daily food intake requirements, especially during the energetically costly breeding season.

Sexual maturation in the Willow warbler occurs relatively quickly for a migratory bird, with the onset of puberty documented at 39 days after hatching [tp = 39 days after hatching] when measured at a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This rapid attainment of reproductive capacity is an adaptation to the species' annual cycle, where young birds from early broods must be physiologically capable of migrating and potentially breeding in the following spring. The 39-day interval from hatching to puberty is relatively short compared to that of many other sylviid warblers, reflecting a life history strategy that prioritizes early maturation to maximize the probability of recruitment into the breeding population. Despite this early physiological readiness, most juvenile birds do not actually attempt to breed in their first calendar year, as they must first complete a demanding trans-Saharan migration and establish a territory upon return. The timing of gonadal activation is therefore linked closely to the photoperiodic cues and nutritional condition of the young bird as it prepares for its first autumn migration.

Under the active metabolic conditions associated with a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the time since birth at first brood is approximately 365 days since birth [tR = approximately 365 days since birth], meaning that most individuals do not breed until their second calendar year of life. This delay between the attainment of puberty at 39 days and the actual first breeding attempt at one year of age reflects the constraints imposed by the species' migratory life history, as young birds must over-winter in sub-Saharan Africa and return to their breeding grounds before they can secure a territory and attract a mate. This pattern contrasts with some resident passerines that can breed in the summer of their birth year. The annual reproductive output is thus limited, with a maximum daily reproduction rate equivalent to 6.5 eggs per 365-day cycle [Ri = daily reproduction rate equivalent to 6.5 eggs per 365-day cycle] for a single female, a value that accounts for the typical clutch size of six to seven eggs produced once per year.

Longevity records for the Willow warbler indicate a maximum lifespan in the wild of approximately 4,307 days [am = approximately 4,307 days], a figure derived from ringing recoveries and calculated at a standard active metabolic temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This translates to roughly 11.8 years of potential survival, making it a relatively long-lived species for such a small passerine. The combination of a single annual breeding event [F_R_i = single annual breeding event] and an extended lifespan suggests a life history strategy that buffers against years of poor reproductive success through iteroparity and adult survival. The relatively high investment per brood, evidenced by the 10 gram [Wwi = 10 gram] adult mass being only about ten times the hatchling mass of 1.05 grams [Wwb = 1.05 grams], indicates that each clutch represents a substantial energetic outlay for the parents. The species' longevity is further supported by its migratory strategy, which reduces exposure to harsh northern winters but introduces significant mortality risks during the biannual crossing of the Sahara Desert and the Mediterranean Sea.
